question: Can reward modeling be cast as a reasoning task, and what training recipe makes a generative reward model reason well enough to beat scalar and larger generative RMs?
hypothesis: Integrating long reasoning chains into reward modeling significantly improves RM interpretability and performance.
contributions: Show reasoning abilities are crucial for reward models and formulate reward modeling as a reasoning process.
A distillation + RL training recipe producing RM-R1 models (7B to 32B) that beat larger models by up to 4.9% on average.
A systematic empirical study of training recipes for reasoning reward models.

method.summary: Generative pairwise reward model trained in two stages: SFT on ~8.7K long reasoning traces (Claude-3.7-Sonnet, corrected by o3) with a Chain-of-Rubrics format, then GRPO with a +1/-1 correctness reward on 64K preference pairs. Reasoning-distilled bases (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen) skip distillation and get RLVR on full data.

limits: Authors concede long CoT outputs raise inference latency (App J); they argue it can be hidden by overlapping rollout and reward computation.
No seeds, variance or significance tests reported; evaluation decoding settings not stated.
Table 3 does not name the model size; the RM-R1 row matches the 32B Instruct row.
Instruct-14B average (77.8) is below INF-ORM-70B (78.8); the headline claim holds only for the Distilled-14B and the 32B models. Abstract 'up to 4.9%' is not tied to a specific cell.
RewardBench alone: best scalar INF-ORM-70B (95.1) beats all RM-R1 models (max 91.4).
Distillation relies on proprietary teachers (Claude-3.7-Sonnet, o3); the traces are teacher-selected using the gold label, so they are rationalisations.
Lemma 1/Prop 1 (App K) is a stylised argument for why RL beats SFT, not a measurement.
